title: Lydia and the jailer (Acts 16)
hookLine: a purple-cloth businesswoman opens her home; a jailer finds Paul and Silas singing at midnight

cards: Two people, one city, and they could hardly be more different. The city is Philippi, a Roman colony in northern Greece. Paul and Silas have crossed the sea after Paul dreamed of a man begging, come over and help us.
On the Sabbath they go down to the river, to a place of prayer, and talk with the women there. One is a businesswoman, a dealer in purple cloth, a costly fabric.
The other, later in the same chapter, is a prison guard, standing in the dark with a sword. Both end the story with the same people at their table.

teach.b: Here's Luke on the first, in the King James Bible: "Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened."

She's a foreigner, a merchant, and a woman who runs her own household; she's baptized with everyone in it. Then she won't take no for an answer: come into my house, and stay. Luke says she constrained them.
Her home becomes the believers' meeting place in Philippi. Now the other side of town. Paul drives a spirit out of a slave girl whose fortune-telling earned her owners money, and they're furious.
They drag Paul and Silas to the magistrates.
The two are stripped, beaten with rods, and thrown into the inner prison with their feet in the stocks, bleeding, in the dark.
Then: "at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them." An earthquake shakes the prison, the doors fly open, everyone's chains come loose.
The jailer wakes, sees the open doors, and draws his sword to kill himself, sure his prisoners have fled.
Paul shouts: "Do thyself no harm: for we are all here." Nobody ran.

teach.h: AT MIDNIGHT PAUL AND SILAS SANG.
teach.b: The jailer falls down trembling and asks, what must I do to be saved? That night he washes their wounds, he and his household are baptized, and sets food before them, rejoicing.
A merchant's house and a jailer's house, both opened in one chapter, and the hinge is two beaten men singing in the dark.

how: Many Christians sing hymns and psalms in hard times, and some prison ministries point to Paul and Silas singing at midnight. Lydia is honored as a saint by Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches.

o: plain wool woven for a shepherd's coat
the nets fishermen mended beside the lake
a costly dyed fabric Lydia sold for a living

games.q: who said or did what — tap the pairs.
p: a seller of purple from Thyatira
drew his sword to kill himself

s: the prisoners escaped when the doors opened
nobody ran. Paul shouted, do thyself no harm: for we are all here.
Lydia's house became a meeting place for the church
she insisted they stay, and before leaving the city Paul and Silas meet the believers in her house.
Paul and Silas sang after they were set free
they sang at midnight, beaten, with their feet in the stocks, and the prisoners heard them.

games.q: you're Paul. an earthquake has opened every door and loosed every chain. the jailer is about to fall on his sword. what do you do?
o: slip out quietly while you can.
shout to him: do yourself no harm, we're all here.
wait to see what the magistrates decide.
games.why: Paul cries out: do thyself no harm: for we are all here. that night the jailer washes their wounds and feeds them.

practice: Think of a hard thing you're in now, big or small, and let it be there. Then hum a line of something that's ever steadied you, a hymn, a lullaby, anything; it doesn't have to be good, Paul and Silas weren't auditioning.
If you pray, you can let the song be your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Purple cloth. The costly fabric Lydia traded in, a businesswoman whose heart the Lord opened, and who opened her whole house to Paul and Silas. This week: Stephen the martyr, a chariot, a road, Ananias, a Gentile's door, Rhoda, and a song at midnight.

orig.note: Greek: a seller of purple, Luke's one-word job title for Lydia. Purple cloth was a luxury.

carryVoice: Your line: sing at midnight. Tomorrow, Paul quotes the poets of Athens. That's twelve weeks on the path.
